speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The government's failure to resolve disputes in the Post Office appears likely to disrupt postal services to all Canadians. Since legislation appears to be the only way to protect the public interest, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale):
That the government introduce, today, emergency legislation that will ensure continuation of the postal service and continuation of negotiation; and that the House leaders of all parties meet immediately to arrange for the House of Commons to deal with that legislation in all stages today.

subsubtopic: CUTBACKS IN RETRAINING PROGRAMS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, in order to seek the unanimous consent of the House for the following motion. In light of the fact that among the budget cuts announced on September 8 by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) were cuts of some $62.5 million in funds for several Manpower retraining programs, and that these cutbacks reduce the level of support for adult education retraining programs to the level where many people, especially married women with children at home, will be unable to take advantage of them, I move,
seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the President of the Treasury Board be informed by this House that it finds such cuts at a time of rising unemployment to be unacceptable, and that he be instructed to rescind these cuts and to restore the level of funding to all Manpower retraining programs to the level that prevailed before his announcement.

subsubtopic: EXPLOITATION OF OFFSHORE RESOURCES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the continuing refusal of the federal government to deal with Atlantic provinces, like Newfoundland, in a more equitable way in recognizing their historic and legal claims over their social and economic destiny with respect to development of offshore resources, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan):
That the Prime Minister and his cabinet modify their policies in this respect to recognize the rights of the provinces to develop and exploit offshore mineral and petroleum resources, which will be done in any event as in the case of the western provinces, under the aegis of national energy policy guidelines, National Energy Board regulations and environmental policy.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising from the refusal of someone on the other side of the House to allow the motion of the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott).
Questions have been asked in the House, on numerous occasions, about the squandering of public money on the Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere project. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has always said that this giveaway was good value. Now that the Senate Standing Committee on National Finance has studied the matter thoroughly and concluded that the government lost its shirt, it is time for this House to see that everything is done to get to the bottom of this gross waste of public funds. That in view of the statement of the Senate finance committee in the report entitled "The Accommodation Program of the Department of Public Works" that "the decision to proceed appears to have rested on other than purely economic considerations", this House requests the establishment of a royal commission on government accommodation procurement procedures with particular reference to all negotiations and agreements leading to the lease-purchase agreement for Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere complex in Hull.

The Prime Minister will recall that his Postmaster General-who is occasionally in the House-gave the clear undertaking that he would be prepared to meet his responsibilities. We gather that means to ensure that the mail is delivered and to act as quickly as possible.
Since we now know that this morning mail service stopped in Charlottetown, Montreal, Windsor and Calgary, with a threat of more stoppages to come, will the Prime Minister today introduce emergency legislation in this House to guarantee the continuation of postal service and also guarantee the continuation of negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

We hope they will call off the strike, which is premature in the sense it was not called by the union executive. If they do, then the question of the Leader of the Opposition remains hypothetical. If they do not call it off, the government will have to take very urgent steps indeed.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was in the process of pointing out an obvious fact and truth about the leaders' day presentation. We witnessed a situation where the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) gave a prime ministerial direction, an inspiring address about the direction in which he felt the country should be headed. On the other hand we had the unusual situation where we found the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) again preoccupied with carping criticism. As the former vice-president of the United States, Mr. Spiro Agnew, once said about a certain enemy of his, "He was a nattering nabob of negativism".
Canadians have had enough of this Prime Minister and the manner in which on every occasion, whenever there is a difficult time or difficult issue to face, he rises and acts as the critic and complains about the proposals of other people, blames Canadians, the press, or anyone he can; but accepts absolutely no responsibility for his leadership as Prime Minister of the country. I commend my own leader for the manner in which he filled the void we have in Canada and in parliament, as far as presenting concrete, constructive, and positive proposals for the recovery of our economy and our national unity.

speechtext:
I should like to continue with my observations concerning why we are here at this time. We are faced with an unexpected parliament, a time when most of us thought we would have an opportunity to place our positions before Canadians. It is a parliament which was called by a Prime Minister who, quite frankly, was afraid to deal with the electorate at this time because of a certainty of being defeated at the polls.
The Address-Mr. Hnatyshyn
At the conclusion of my remarks last night I was making the suggestion that what we need now is an election to clear the air, with an opportunity for a new mandate. The problem resulting from the extension of this parliament is, and continues to be, that the proposals by the government in power at this time tend to be those very heavily weighted in favour of political consideration. Regardless of who the victor is at the polls, I am certain that, following such an election, a new government would have the opportunity of introducing an economic plan, as an example, in the context of carrying the plan forward over a period of four or four and a half years. I am sure that we in this party will have that opportunity as a result of being successful.
All we have before us now in the Speech from the Throne is a series of suggested so-called cutbacks, completely out of context with what we need in this country at this time. My leader pointed out that we need not only a period of restraint but some fundamental changes in terms of government restraint. On the other hand we require some economic stimulus in order to get our economy moving, to increase our productivity performance, bringing us back into a competitive position with other industrialized nations of the world.
The fact of the matter is that the options open to this government and this parliament are severely and seriously limited. We simply do not have any room in which to operate. This government, when it intends to make fundamental changes, must always consider the political consequences. Therefore it is unable to bring forward the kind of fundamental program my leader outlined in his speech yesterday, and to which the Prime Minister took such great exception in that most negative and unfortunate demonstration he put on here in the House yesterday.
Let me recall to the memory of hon. members of the House that at the time of the last election the Prime Minister made a great issue of the question of leadership. He is again in the position of a sort of macho figure, standing on the train platform, indicating the kind of leadership he could give as opposed to that of the Leader of the Opposition. He did that in respect of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) in the past. I am sure hon. members on the other side have been hearing the same things I have heard, about how unfortunate it was that the hon. member for Halifax did not have the opportunity to serve as prime minister as opposed to the man now filling that post.
At the last campaign the man who has led our country into the position in which it now finds itself used the same tactics he displayed yesterday in the House. He believes he can go back to that well a number of times, using the same tactics. Let me inform the Prime Minister in no uncertain terms that, from my reading of the electorate, I am sure this particular ploy will not work again, except, perhaps, with those rapidly diminishing hard-bitten supporters he has in this country who still have some faith in the Prime Minister and his party.
In his speech yesterday afternoon the Prime Minister indicated, at least to me, a certain desperateness, particularly

In my estimation the Prime Minister is withdrawing more and more from a consideration of advice, and is becoming more than preoccupied with the whole matter of constitutional reform. This is indicated by the urgency of implementation and the arbitrary deadline set and reiterated by him again yesterday. This whole matter has become an obsession with him. It is my belief that he intends to move in this area, notwithstanding the consequences to the country, with the idea that somehow only he should have the opportunity to decide what kind of a constitution we should have in Canada.
Let me point out the danger inherent in this attitude demonstrated by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is becoming more and more isolated, particularly in matters relating to the constitution and matters concerning the economy of our country. He has become more and more withdrawn, seeking the advice of perhaps only two or three people on his own staff. He no longer consults to any degree with his cabinet. His cabinet colleagues have become superfluous to the whole process. What we are observing in Canada is a breakdown of what we term the traditional parliamentary cabinet system.
Incidentally, I was amazed yesterday to hear the Prime Minister's comments as to how the hand applause from this side was a terrible departure from British parliamentary tradition. Apparently the Prime Minister is unaware that in the United Kingdom members do not have desks to pound. That fact has obviously escaped his attention. Of course, he attempts in his rhetoric here to be an expert. He tries to appear or pretend to be knowledgeable on all such matters.
We have observed this obvious breakdown of cabinet government under this Prime Minister. What have been the consequences of that breakdown? I suggest there are four basic consequences. One of the great virtues of cabinet government is that its structure lends itself to decision-making after all the major points of view have been considered. The quality of decision depends on the extent of prior adversary discussion. When discussion formerly took place in full cabinet it was likely that most of the available options were considered.
What we have now is unilateral action by this Prime Minister. He has made apparently serious statements on national television about the future destiny of this country in terms of the economy, without prior consultation with members of his cabinet. This fact is supported by the surprise shown by

cabinet ministers on being told about his statement, and by the bumbling and stumbling effort of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to justify the position adopted by the government in the last months.
This withdrawal from the traditional practice of cabinet government in our country, together with his authoritarian, arrogant, and insular attitude, has resulted in a reduction of consultation with his own cabinet to almost none. Members of his own party sit back, not to their credit, and continue to support this man with his non-consultative leadership.
We do not have to speculate about his supporters' attitude toward his actions in terms of the constitution. A long-time supporter of the Prime Minister's party, Senator Lang, outlined this very eloquently at the Joint Committee on the Constitution. He said that the constitutional proposals in the bill were never discussed in Liberal caucus at any time prior to presentation by the Prime Minister in this House. That is the kind of consultation we get from the Prime Minister. That is the shoddy way in which he treats the backbenchers in his party as well as his cabinet ministers. As a result, they are now becoming a laughing stock in terms of government throughout the world.
Where is this sense of leadership that we have heard about? Where is this great Prime Minister leading us to, aside from his carping and criticism at the first opportunity he has to demonstrate leadership when he comes into this House and gives us no specific, constructive direction as a country? We got nothing but an act which did him shame.
Cabinet government has meant in the past that cabinet has had to contain a number of able and strong-minded ministers who have the trust and confidence of the Prime Minister. In this changed reality it seems no longer to be a political advantage to have strong and able ministers in the cabinet, but rather something of a disadvantage to this Prime Minister. Such a man seems to interfere with the plans and wishes of the Prime Minister and his personal entourage. This is why, in the last three to four years, we have had the situation where one after the other of the stronger-that is a relative term respecting this government-ministers left this particular cabinet. It is hardly assuring that the most prominent departing ministers were those responsible for the government departments dealing with the finances and economy of our country.
1 recall very vividly the umbrage taken by a past minister of finance, I believe it was Mr. Turner, when the Prime Minister surrounded himself with his own set of economists, the group of seven, and simply superseded the advice and decisions made by the minister's office and Department of Finance officials. This is the kind of leadership that this man gives.
In a federal country the minister has always had a role to play in representing his region. The danger with the breakdown we are now experiencing in cabinet rule in this country is that, more and more, we find the situation where ministers are having less and less influence in the important decisions with respect to our country. It is no wonder we are suffering the
October 13, 1978

greatest stresses with respect to regional dissatisfaction that we have ever experienced in the history of our country in the time that we have had this government in office.
Cabinet solidarity is an important concept which has gone by the board with this government. Cabinet solidarity is important because it means that the decisions made, notwithstanding their difficulty, have only been arrived at after difficult, internal, adversary discussion. We have lost that now and are being ruled by one man and a small clique of his own personal staff which he has built up consistently since he came into office, a rather elaborate and large apparatus in his own department.
I want to deal briefly, Mr. Speaker, in the time I have available to me, with some other examples of the kind of leadership and disgraceful performance put on by the Prime Minister yesterday afternoon, a time when he had the opportunity to deal with current issues of some importance. We in western Canada have been forgotten and left out absolutely in the Speech from the Throne. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) may smile, but he well understands that there are serious problems in western Canada because he is one who has had a long association with that part of the country. The fact of the matter is that there was no attention whatsoever paid to the important matters relating to transportation when you consider the grain transportation problems we are facing and the way in which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is attempting to undermine the excellent recommendations of the Hall commission. It is a disgrace that there is nothing set forward in this extended parliament by the government with respect to the difficulties we are experiencing in grain movement.
Another example of the Prime Minister's poor leadership is the way he has handled the resource issues, the way in which he simply and arbitrarily dismissed the right of the Atlantic provinces to offshore resources and minerals. This was an insult to every person and coastal province in this country. The Prime Minister will be extremely sorry, notwithstanding the rhetoric of the position he took yesterday which was further evidence of his arrogant and, indeed, impudent attitude toward both sides and both ends of this country. He has written off Atlantic and western Canada. He understands now that he must concentrate on seeking support in the two central provinces or he will be gone, and that is what we will be seeing in this parliament. We will be seeing an absolute dismissal of these two important regions, Atlantic and western Canada.
What about the Post Office, Mr. Speaker? What kind of leadership has he given there? On August 1 he was full of vim and vigour, "We are going to act with respect to the Post Office." They have done nothing but taunt the union in question, CUPW. They put big ads in the paper saying to the effect, "What a bunch of buffoons these people are for making these demands." Is that the kind of leadership we want, an attempt to create a confrontation before a parliamentary session so that the Prime Minister can walk into parliament and say, "Here is legislation, bring them back to work"? Is that strength in leadership?

The way this government has dealt with the provinces with respect to taxation matters in resource areas has led to some serious questions with respect to provincial rights in the resource field. speechtext:
1 did not put my money in the Bank of Western Canada which was promoted some years ago by an hon. member on the other side of the House. I had more faith in western Canada.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, one thing is clear in this debate and will probably run through the entire thirtieth parliament, and that is that we have a healthy economy and a strong, confident, private sector in our country. We will be taking a number of measures to assist private enterprise as we believe that it can effectively do the job and provide many,

many more permanent jobs in Canada. Certainly we intend to give responsible leadership, and I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) demonstrated that in his speech yesterday. Certainly it was an expression of confidence, not like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who, as I said, puffed himself up from time to time with one complaint after another, and seemed to have a split personality. Not long ago I read about somebody who had 12 personalities and woke up and found himself another person. I would not accuse the Leader of the Opposition of having twelve personalities; as my colleague here suggests, he has not even got one good one. I guess that is true.
Confidence and responsible leadership go together. The business community is becoming more and more confident, as can be seen in investment figures and surveys of investment intentions in this country because this government has demonstrated that it is committed to assisting private business growth. We have done so in a number of ways which add up to a co-ordinated set of policy directions toward a growth oriented economy. As a result, while unemployment and inflation still are too high, Canada is working its way through the difficult world economic problems better than are most countries. Certainly the Prime Minister dealt with that subject at length yesterday. It was nice to see some honest admission of this fact instead of the old myths that we cannot be competitive and that our industry is not competitive with the rest of the world. Instead of crying the blues, as we hear from time to time from the other side of the House, it was nice to see someone admit their confidence in the businessmen of Canada and say that businessmen are not a group of dummies who must have their hands held when they go to the bathroom. I would rather build confidence than confusion.
Another myth spread by the "fearful Freddies" opposite is that our businessmen cannot compete, unless it is in raw resources, because they are too backward, too inefficient, too unsophisticated in their products. I will be releasing in a few days a factual study of Canada's export performance from 1960 to 1977. It will make remarkable reading, and I commend it to members of the opposition parties.
They talk all the time over there about our rising deficit on so-called end products or fully manufactured goods yet our exports of end products have increased much faster than our imports of end products. In 1977 we exported nearly 20 times more of end products than we exported in 1960; we imported in 1977 less than five times the imports of end products in I960. Instead of a rising deficit in end products, it has fallen from about 21 per cent of our total trade turnover-exports plus imports-in 1960, to 12.7 per cent in 1977.
Canadian export growth was stronger than the world average during that period that we studied, the period from 1960 to 1977 when the average annual increase of Canadian exports was 13.2 per cent, which is certainly far higher than the growth of the total economy. This is of vital importance to Canada when we consider how important export trade is to our country in relation to other countries. Approximately 25 per cent of our GNP is dependent upon our exports. If we wanted
October 13, 1978

to relate that to what many people consider to be the great trading nation of the world, Japan, it must be noted that 13 per cent of their GNP is dependent upon exports. In the United States less than 6 per cent of their GNP is dependent on exports.
We must and we have paid strict attention to our exports, and we can be proud of the rate of growth of the export of finished products over the years.
Over the same period there has been a strong shift in the composition of our exports toward manufactured goods, with a decline in the shares of farm exports and metal ores. There has been a major increase in the export orientation of Canadian manufacturing at the same time as we have had an increase in imports of manufactured goods. Without trying to present too many statistics to the House today, I would point out that the proportion of our trade in manufactured form rose steadily from 8 per cent in 1960 to 46 per cent in 1977. This shows the steady increase in our ability to sell fully manufactured goods on the world market. The share of manufactured products as a whole, including fabricated goods such as aluminum ingots, rose from 60 per cent in 1960 to 77 per cent in 1977.
Last year alone this country exported $1.3 billion worth of machinery and equipment to the developing world, not to mention billions of dollars worth to the United States, Europe and Japan. We are out there and we are active. Probably no other industrial country in the past 15 years has seen so remarkable a transformation of its commodity trade pattern, and all the while our timid friends opposite were saying that Canadian businessmen could not hack it. Some of them are even saying we must go back to being hewers of wood and drawers of water. We need no longer depend upon that fact at all. While I have nothing against hewers of wood and drawers of water, it is clearly recognizable that you cannot employ too many people if you confine yourself to those types of industry, and we are not.
Let us talk about industrial output and the use of the International Monetary Fund and the OECD as our sources. Since before the recession of 1973-74, Canada and the United States have had about the same growth in industrial output, that is, mining, manufacturing and utilities. This is far ahead of any other major industrial nation, and far ahead of all of our largest export markets.
From 1973 to 1978 we have been second only to Japan, and not by much in growth in our gross national product in real terms. We have had by far the strongest growth in employment of any industrial country, and the Prime Minister dealt with those figures yesterday. Even in prices we have done better than most industrial countries. West Germany has done better, and the United States moderately better.
Those are Canadian businessmen out there, scoring remarkable achievements. Certainly they deserve some confidence from the politicians, and we are prepared to give them all the confidence we can. We have confidence that they really know what they are doing and that they can do their jobs best. What
The Address-Mr. Horner
are their opportunities? They have useful views as to what the government can do to help them so nearly a year ago I went to the private sector and the provinces to find out what the most responsible actions would be for the federal and provincial governments to take in order to encourage industrial growth.
We set up 23 individual industry sector task forces composed of business and labour, with the provinces and the federal government having modest representation. They have sent their reports to me and to the provincial ministers of industry. The federal government is now going over all of them with a fine tooth comb.
A second committee has been composed strictly of senior business and labour executives, along with a neutral academic. They are assessing the complete role of the 23 sector reports in order to draw out the common threads of policy recommendations. The second tier committee report will be coming to me very shortly, and naturally it will be sent to the provincial ministers as soon as possible. In fact, we expect it next week.
Federal and provincial deputy ministers of industry will be discussing the second tier and the sector reports in a few weeks. Provincial ministers and myself will follow their example early in November, and the first ministers of Canada will be meeting at the end of November to discuss and identify the policy recommendations that are made. All of this, in my opinion, is a responsible and competent building agenda for action, based upon the best assessment of men and women out there as to what government can do, or can stay out of, to help them grow.
While this process was going on, the government was moving in areas where there already was a consensus that changes were needed, and indeed, the views of the individual sector reports found expression in our recent economic announcements.
Hon. members know from the screams they hear that the government is seriously cutting back its spending, and cutting back the size and intervention of the public service. Most of the screams are coming from the other side, which cries out for cutting government spending but which whimpers when, inevitably, someone is hurt.
Hon. members know that federal government employment is being held at zero growth. However, some layoffs are occuring. Public service salaries will be legislated to prevent them outpacing those in the private sector. The Economic Council of Canada is working at practical means to try to reduce the extent and cost of government regulation to industry. We are spending more on job creation with money saved through the more selective application of unemployment insurance payments and family allowances.
In the past year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) introduced means and measures to stimulate employment, production, and investment, for example, the reduction of sales taxes, extension of the investment tax credit, the introduction of wage subsidies, and the incentives for industrial R and D. My own department and agencies reporting to me have made very large increases in our support to Canadian industry. I

The Address-Mr. Horner
might mention we are assisting Canadian industry in all parts of Canada, including western Canada. We have done a great deal to help the oil and gas industry, particularly in Alberta, within the last year.
The announcements made by the Prime Minister, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), and the Minister of Finance, in August were a further demonstration of our commitment to economic growth and prudent management. The Minister of Finance announced total new cash outlays of $300 million in 1979-80 in support of economic development. There will be $65 million in new money for tourism and the resource industries. There will be about $28 million for industrial support programs, about $70 million for shipbuilding and repair facilities, and further amounts of money for more major capital projects.
I have taken some time to illustrate the responsible and the united or co-ordinated nature of the government's economic approach, Mr. Speaker. Reducing the economic shares of the country demanded by government, freeing resources to give private enterprise more room, providing supportive government policies in an attempt to improve investment confidence, all these were objectives worked out by federal departments together. The policies mesh, and they mesh within the context of six main policy directions that this government keeps before it. It is a framework for upgrading the position of the private sector as our economy heads into the competitive challenges of the 1980s.
First, Canadian growth and expansion should be fuelled as much as possible by private Canadian funds. That means government restraint and budget cutting will continue to free more resources for yet more growth.
Second, government policies, both provincial and federal, must be directed at growth. 1 am talking about a whole range of policies regulating quality control, environmental issues, competition, intellectual property, and paper burden requirements. The federal government will protect the legitimate objectives of these policies, but we will strive to design them to keep to a minimum the constraints on industrial growth.
Third, we will see that the required economic infrastructure is in place. This will include transportation facilities such as roads, harbours, railways, pipelines, power and energy facilities. We will contribute in three ways: we will facilitate and speed up the approval of private sector projects for the Alcan pipeline; we will increase our support for infrastructure projects through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion; we will make direct contributions to certain important projects. A list of major projects which could move ahead in the next two years is being reviewed.
Fourth, to be successful in the competitive 1980s, Canada will need very highly trained and skilled manpower. Federal manpower training programs are being revised to increase substantially the amount of skills and on-the-job training support. We are working on improving manpower mobility in Canada.
Fifth, because of the dependence upon new technology for future growth, the government has already enriched its R and D incentives in the tax systems. Now we are committed to a further program that will increase Canada's R and D expenditures toward 1.5 per cent of the gross national product in the early 1980s. The program will be designed to ensure that most of the new R and D will be done within industry itself.
Sixth, and maybe closest to my heart today, is the improvement of industrial support programs and services. I will complete my speech by expanding upon this point.

Before some members opposite run off and say that we are spending $1 billion, I want to emphasize that what we are doing is insuring loans that the banks make to enterprises which can prove that they are justified. We insure 90 per cent of the loan and, in some cases, if it is an innovative, new idea, 100 per cent.
This is an expression of confidence by this government in the business community and in their ability to meet the challenges of the eighties. This might be called last resort financing in the form of government loss insurance for loans made by private lending institutions. Since it is a revolving authority, as loans are repaid new insurance can be provided. As a result, more than $1 billion will be made available in term debt to help companies expand or go into new activity.
I might say that last year some 256 companies were helped by this program. Only seven of those 256 were not of Canadian ownership. I want to point that out, because we are helping Canadians. It is an expression of confidence by Canadians in the Canadian economy that we are helping.
The enterprise development board is a central board. It is here in Ottawa. In addition, we have set up ten boards in the provinces, all led by businessmen who spend their funds through direct loans and grants and also through such high level devices as loan guarantees and risk insurance. An additional $28 million for 1979-80 will actually provide support to the industry of about $100 million. Through the first half of the next ten years, it is projected that the funds will provide more than $1.3 billion worth of support.
The enterprise development program, of course, is not all that the federal government does to encourage industry in Canada. As I mentioned, the Export Development Corporation, the Federal Business Development Bank and the Small Businesses Loans Act, together with the Department of Trade's other services, in 1977-78 provided support to Canadian industry of $3.7 billion and were directly involved in 197,000 projects, mostly smaller and medium-sized businesses in Canada.
A new and improved enterprise development program will broaden this criteria to include more smaller and mediumsized businesses. My colleague, the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) has been successful in arguing their case. He will now have the enjoyable job of explaining to small businessmen what there is and how they can get it.
The flexibility of the enterprise development program to encourage mergers and acquisitions will be increased by several new measures. Support for research, design, and development is going up markedly. More money is being provided for export market development and sales promotion, particularly in areas of the United States. The department will implement a $100 million contingency liability authority to provide risk re-insurance that will further assist Canadian companies to participate in major capital projects.
There are several other measures, all geared to assist business in Canada, to streamline, modernize, and grasp the opportunities. We are entering a period of great change in

In the short time remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I shall attempt to sum up what I have been saying, and make a few further comments upon our economic performance and potential.
As I said, we are entering upon a period of great change in technology, trading patterns, and consumer demand, and we do so with many strengths both in resources and expertise. Some have expressed a lack of confidence in the businessmen of Canada, but we on this side certainly have great confidence in them. We recognize that as a result of freer trade some Canadian firms may find themselves in difficulties. However, we expect that more opportunities than difficulties will arise as a result of negotiations. The lower tariff barriers and the removal of non-tariff barriers in Japan, United States and Europe, will definitely help Canadian business firms and improve the economic climate. The industrial support I have outlined has been designed to assist companies to restructure themselves so as minimize difficulties which may be foreseen in the early 1980s.
We will be setting up a special MTN-related panel to advise the enterprise development program as to which particular industries will be hurt and the way in which we can help those industries to take advantage of the lower tariffs which may come about as a result of the negotiations. I believe that any who read my speech carefully would agree we have been showing tremendous economic leadership over the whole range of Canadian industry. We have received the co-operation of labour-some 40 different unions have worked on the production of those task force reports and most of the provinces have also been involved in their preparation. We are engaged in a concentrated effort to help Canadian businessmen because we believe the private sector is really the engine by which economic recovery and development will be brought about, along with an extensive effort by my department toward trade promotion.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) mentioned my visit to Japan. As hon. members know, I went to Japan and

October 13, 1978
The Address-Mr. Crouse
Korea this summer and was greatly heartened by what I saw, by evidence of our opportunity to increase sales to Japan. Recently, with the help of my department, an extensive, high-powered group of Canadian businessmen visited mainland China. They have reported to me in detail concerning their hopes for additional sales to China.
Canadians concerned with oil exploration both from the private sector and Petro-Can formed part of the group which made that business trip, and they believe a tremendous amount of good will flow from that visit. Intensive work is being done in Indonesia as well as in many countries of South America. Trade shows and trade promotion throughout the world have made people more fully aware of the competence of Canadian businessmen and of their ability to compete in international markets. As one example I might refer to an article which I saw in a newspaper only this morning-Canada is selling cameras to Japan. That certainly sounds like sending coals to Newcastle, I suppose, but it is certainly evidence of our competence and capability.
Much remains to be done, of course. We are working very hard in connection with the automobile industry, the biggest single employer in the province of Ontario. We are devoting a great deal of attention to the shipbuilding and repair industry on both the east and the west coasts. Everybody knows there is an overcapacity in the world as far as shipbuilding is concerned but we can, and should, nevertheless, improve our facilities so that we can carry out a good deal of the repair work which is necessary to enable the shipping industry to move our goods throughout the world.
I end by expressing my confidence that the business community will appreciate what we are doing. We shall continue to work with them. Meetings are to be held later this month involving my provincial counterparts in both industry and tourism. Canada is healthy, well, and working.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on the throne speech, and my first words will be to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address who, through their presentation, did honour to their constituencies.
"A Tale of Two Cities" by Charles Dickens was first published as a volume in 1859, some 119 years ago. In chapter one of this classic story, Dickens wrote:
It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair. We had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to heaven, we were all going direct the other way.
Although published in 1859, Dickens used these words to describe conditions in 1775 as they existed then between the people in Europe who spoke English and those in Europe who spoke French. His words pointed out the national disorder which existed.
Unfortunately, things have not improved very much since those days. The words of Dickens in 1859 could well be used today to describe aptly conditions in Canada as they exist at present. We have a throne speech opening the fourth session of the thirtieth parliament which is repetitive and misleading. I say it is repetitive for it speaks of strengthening the economy and of helping the private sector to lead the way toward accelerated economic growth. We have known about this requirement for many years. In fact the government has been saying the same thing for some time, but unfortunately no action has been taken.
For example, on February 17, 1972, the throne speech stated the following:
This country fails in its essential purpose if it does not ensure that its most precious resource, human talent, is not wasted away.
How very true those words are!
On January 4, 1973, the throne speech stated:
It is timely to provide to parliament a full report on Canada's financial and economic situation and to propose fiscal and other measures for the effective management of the economy.
On October 18, 1977, the throne speech stated:
The human hardship imposed by the current level of unemployment in Canada is deeply disturbing in that there should be so many men and women deprived of the dignity of self-supporting work, unable to meet their financial commitments and plan confidently for the future.
Obviously the present Liberal government while in office was well aware of the problems, but unfortunately it took no corrective action during the past ten years.
I say the throne speech is misleading because it states:
The projected rate of expenditure growth during the next fiscal year is 8.9 per cent, which is well below the forecast growth of 11 per cent for the gross national product.
It is this type of economic governmental double talk over the years which has brought Canada to the brink of economic ruin. The Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) own pledge of a 5 per cent economic growth as made at the Bonn economic summit is now open to question. I say it is open to question because all of the economists in this country and all the financial papers in this country tell us that we will do well if the rate of growth achieved is at around 4 per cent, not the 5 per cent pledged by the Prime Minister or the 11 per cent stated in the throne speech.
What we are witnessing today is a cruel con job on the Canadian people perpetrated by the present Trudeau Liberal government. In the throne speech we are told that the government will intensify its assault upon unemployment and inflation, carrying forward commitments made by the government in 1976 with the publication of "The Way Ahead". Time will not permit me to deal today with all the words of good intent, the pledges and promises broken since the present Liberal government printed the booklet entitled "The Way Ahead". Obviously the government knew the problems and their cure, as witnessed by the words on page eight, paragraph two, under the heading of "Inflationary Process", which read:
Increased government spending can lead to higher prices if the government simply prints the money or if additional taxes levied to finance these expendi-

October 13, 1978

tures are passed on to others through higher wages and prices. Excessively high wage settlements and pricing decisions impose higher levels of cost, leading directly to higher prices. Expectations escalate and inflation continues to feed upon itself.
The debilitating effects of inflation extend beyond economic considerations to threaten the very nature of our institutions and traditions. The problems that unrestricted inflation creates were spelled out in the budget speech of June 23, 1975:
-inflation ultimately inflicts grievous damage to the fabric of society. It lowers the living standards of those on fixed incomes, including pensioners. It leaves people without reliable, understandable guideposts by which to arrange their economic affairs. It injects grave uncertainty into decisions on family budgets, housing, savings and provision for old age. It provokes deep frustration, social tension and mistrust of private and public institutions. Collective bargaining is embittered. Industrial relations are damaged. We in Canada are already beginning to live some of these experiences.
That was printed in October of 1976. Those are the words printed by the Trudeau Liberal government in "The Way Ahead", and yet this government proceeded, under finance minister Turner, finance minister Macdonald, and under the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), to do exactly the opposite.
Obviously this government intentionally kept printing more paper money to cover their blunders in a direct attempt to destroy the Canadian economy. I charge this government with the deliberate destruction of the stability and endurance of our economic system, with the deliberate destruction of the social and cultural traditions on which it is based, for reasons known only to a select clique who sits beside and around the Prime Minister of this country.
I listened to the Prime Minister yesterday when he spent most of his time berating my party, my leader, and our policies, instead of putting some flesh on the bones of his proposals in the throne speech. There is not a word about fisheries development in the throne speech. The Prime Minister could have spent some time telling us of his concern for the fishermen in Atlantic Canada and in the western part of this country and in British Columbia. He said not a word about that.

Senator Eugene Forsey put into words perhaps the most concise and forceful objection to the proposals of the Prime Minister. Yet in September when opening the Nova Scotia Fisheries Exhibition in my home town of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, Mr. Smallwood stated his strong opposition to the constitutional proposals of the government. He stated, to roars of approval from thousands in the exhibition audience, that whenever the next federal election is called, and if he is required to make a choice between his party and the monarchy, he will vote for the Queen.
It is one thing for the Prime Minister to say in this House, with tongue in cheek, that the role of the Queen in his constitutional proposals is unchanged. However, Bill C-60 tells a very different story. I for one do not accept the position of the Prime Minister that there is no need to refer to the Supreme Court proposed changes respecting the monarchy, just because he said that it is not the intention of the government to propose changes of substance.
For example, by clause 30 of Bill C-60 the government states that the sovereign head of Canada is Her Majesty the Queen. But clauses Nos. 42 and 43 provide for the Governor General to represent the Queen and exercise for her the prerogatives, functions and authority belonging to her in respect of Canada. Other clauses of the bill substitute the

October 13, 1978
The Address-Mr. Crouse
Governor General for the Queen. For example, the opening words of clause 91 vest in the Governor General on behalf of the Queen the executive government of and over Canada. I disagree violently with the Prime Minister and the deceitful position which he is taking on this matter. I believe strongly that these proposals contain substantive elements which raise serious questions about the right of the federal government and parliament to act unilaterally on this issue.
Under our present federation, Her Majesty is the head equally of our federal and provincial governments. There is substantial doubt in my mind that her position can be altered by one level of government, especially this lame duck government in the dying stages of this parliament. This is only one matter which is of serious concern to the people in my area.
Another important issue is the ownership of 100 per cent of the mineral rights off the coast of Atlantic Canada. Shortly after assuming the leadership of my party, my leader, without any equivocation or provocation, made it abundantly clear that he would, upon obtaining the position of Prime Minister of this country, give to the Atlantic provinces complete control and the revenues resulting from the development of any oil, gas or mineral discoveries off our shores. Naturally this announcement was greeted with great enthusiasm, not only by the Conservatives in Atlantic Canada but also by the Liberals, and if there were any labour or New Democratic Party members down there, they were rejoicing as well. Why? They were rejoicing because we in Atlantic Canada have found it necessary for years to fight hard for our place in the sun, to fight against the centralizing powers of the federal government and the tariff walls which favoured industry in Ontario and Quebec, while working to the disadvantage of industry in Atlantic Canada.
Everything we buy in Nova Scotia, and in Atlantic Canada generally, costs much more than it does the citizens of Quebec and Ontario due to the 1,500 mile haul from central Canada to our area. The freight rate on automobiles from Oshawa to Halifax makes a difference of approximately $350 in the price paid for a vehicle by a Nova Scotian as compared to residents of Ontario. Truly we in Atlantic Canada are the victims of the ruinous user-pay policy enunciated by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). Over the years we have borne the burden of higher costs, higher freight rates, higher unemployment, and lower scales of wages than the workers of Ontario, Quebec and western Canada. Naturally we had high hopes for any benefits which may accrue to our area as a result of offshore mineral or oil development. However, yesterday as I sat and listened intently to the words of the Prime Minister, I am sure that the high hopes of the citizens of Atlantic Canada could not help but be dampened by his words and attitude. He went out of his way to ridicule and heap scorn upon my leader and my party.

I agree with one of the statements made yesterday by the Prime Minister. He said that they are breaking all records. Well, that is true. Our economy is breaking all records. All records in unemployment are being broken. If the truth were told, there are well over one million people unemployed in this country. All records in inflation are being broken, as well as the records in the devaluation of our currency. All records are being broken in work stoppages, in the flight from Canada of investment capital, in declining productivity, in falling exports, in our soaring national debt and in our budgetary deficits. In these and in all related areas we are indeed exceeding all the other western industrialized countries.
October 13, 1978

It is true that our labour force has had an unusually high growth rate, due in part to the post-war baby boom and continuing immigration. But considering Canada's enormous advantages-we are the second largest land mass in the world, we have coal in every province of this country from British Columbia to Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, we have untapped mineral wealth and every day we are finding new sources of uranium, and we have oil and gas, in fact more natural resources than any other industrialized democracy in the world,-and with a small population, it is surprising we are in our present difficulties. We have substantial production capacity and we should really have no baffling economic problems, and would have none were it not for the crisis this country is suffering today in leadership. We have been like a rudderless ship sailing around in circles; a ship whose captain has lost his sextant, his chart and his compass and does not know which way to turn.
Since we are sinking into a steadily worsening mess, in spite of all Canada's unmatched blessings, the trouble obviously lies with the mismanagement of this country, no matter what the Prime Minister may say to distort the facts and confuse the people. I would ask you, sir, what other explanation can there be for a government which came into power in 1968 when we were a nation of 20 million people?
I hold in my hand a booklet entitled "How Your Tax Dollar Is Spent", put out by C. M. Drury, president of the treasury board in February, 1974. There are many figures here but I am only going to quote one. It shows quite clearly that in 1968 when the present Liberal government under Mr. Trudeau was elected we had 20 million people, and the cost of running this country at that time is shown here as $9,872 million. That was in 1968. Today we have the 1978-79 proposals showing how your tax dollar is spent, brought forward under Robert Andras, President of the Treasury Board. It gives some very interesting figures.
It shows that the 1973-74 expenditures were $24,532 million, an increase of 22.7 per cent in one year. That just happened to be the year that Mr. Turner was minister of finance. It shows that in 1974-75 we were spending $31,483 million. He even outdid himself. He managed a 28.3 per cent increase in that one year. In 1975-76 expenditures went up to $37,278 million, an increase of 18.4 per cent. In 1977-78 expenditures were $44,450 million, an increase of 8.2 per cent, and for this present year, 1978-79, we have total expenditures at $48,800 million, an increase of 9.8 per cent. Those figures have now progressed upwards to something like $50 billion.
These figures clearly indicate the deceit and deception as practised by Liberal speakers when they try to deceive Canadians into believing that during their period in office they have ever practised restraint. The trend of their deceit is evidenced in our declining dollar, our inflationary spiral, and headlines that scream that our small businesses are going bankrupt as never before.
I wish the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) were in the House. I will not say he intentionally
The Address-Mr. Crouse
misled the House, because that would be unfair. I would say that in his ignorance today he misled the House because he implied that everything was okay with small businessmen. Last year 4,131 Canadian firms were placed in bankruptcy. By way of comparison, the ten times as large U.S. economy had only twice as many failures. The trend has worsened in the first four months of 1978 when Canada had 1,742 business failures as compared with only 2,303 in the United States.
These figures say nothing of the lost hopes, the spent dreams, and the lost lifetime savings of the men and women who worked to put together these businesses. This is a direct result of the mismanagement of our economy by the present Liberal administration. Small businessmen do not have the expertise to deal with currency fluctuation and foreign exchange, or their eventual impact on prices. Unfortunately the figures show that Atlantic Canada again bears a heavy burden with bankruptcies up from 114 in 1976 to 190 in 1977.
Recent government restraint proposals will not, of course, improve the situation. While I am in general agreement that government expenditures must be curtailed, I find it disconcerting, for example, to hear the proposal to close the Vancouver and Halifax fish technology laboratories. This will save the government less than $2 million annually. I find this difficult to understand when at the same time there is no mention of curtailing services at one of our international airports, the deficits on which since it opened in 1976 total $115 million- almost $1 million a week.
The two laboratories in question have served the Canadian fish industry for some 54 years. Their scientists are highly respected not only in Canada but throughout the entire length and breadth of the world. They are respected for their research and development. This action, of course, brings into question the government's entire list of spending priority.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan), for example, when speaking in London, Ontario, on April 4, 1978, stated that Canada's poor performance in industrial innovation is threatening its competitive position in both domestic and foreign markets. He said that research and development are vital to the future of Canada and that some of the issues of most pressing national concern at this moment, such as economic stability, unemployment, and even national unity, are directly linked to our investment in research and development.
Since the Hon. Judd Buchanan holds these views, it is obvious he was not consulted by the Prime Minister before the announcement of the cuts, particularly those that are of vital concern to our fishermen and our processors both in Atlantic Canada and in British Columbia. If he had been consulted I am sure he would not have agreed. This points up the fact that we have almost a dictatorship in this country today-a one-man government under Pierre Elliott Trudeau.
On the east coast the extension of the 200-mile limit, the scarcity of some fish species, the environmental quality regulations, food safety and nutrition, plus the necessity to examine non-traditional markets, non-traditional fishing grounds, and the marketing of non-traditional species, have all placed new

October 13, 1978
The Address-Mr. Crouse
demands on our fisheries laboratories and our scientists. Without basic planning, dismantling the technological laboratories will drive some of the work toward our universities which are understaffed and hard pressed financially. In my opinion this will result in the work becoming fragmented and more and more remote from the practical world of industry.
Our fish exports play an important role by bringing into Canada scarce and vital foreign exchange. Some 75 per cent or more of all the fish we catch is exported, and Canada's need for foreign exchange is greater than it has ever been in our history. We can only export fish profitably by maintaining a high standard of quality, and this can only be done through the aid of our scientists. From a financial point of view, exported product which is rejected by the buyer is a financial loss which must also include the cost of shipping. The reputation of the shipper is at stake, as well as the reputation of Canada.
It is also well to remember that the export market is open to the small processors, as well as the large, and that overseas markets are specialized and require new skills in processing, freezing and packaging which can only be provided by our fisheries scientists, especially for our small processors. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce spoke today of his department's efforts to aid research and development. This will be helpful to the large companies, but without the scientific laboratories to help the small, individual packers and processors, they are bound to go out of business because they cannot compete. This is the problem that the small operator is facing today. At a time when we in Atlantic Canada are seeking new markets for expanding catches, closing the fisheries labs appears to me to be penny wise and pound foolish. No matter how you look at it, we have made one step forward and three backward in our quest for a stronger financial base in Canada as a whole, and Atlantic Canada in particular.
This action, of course, places in doubt the future benefits which should accrue to our people from the extension of our economic zone to 200 miles. To realize the opportunities available from this action, it is necessary to establish a climate leading to continuity of investment. As the Minister of Finance has put it, "We will encourage risk-taking and willingness to spend in the private sector that is essential to get the economy going faster." Unfortunately, to date this has not been done.
In my opinion, there are a number of problems that are not creating a favourable climate for long-term investment.
I will be finished in a moment, Mr. Speaker.
For example, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) has adopted a go-slow, stand-pat attitude toward the fisheries. He wants to wait until fish quotas are plentiful before establishing a long-term policy that would lead to modernizing and rebuilding our inshore, midwater and offshore fleets. We believe such waiting to be detrimental to Canada's interests, and we are not alone in this belief. A spokesman from one of our leading processors has publicly stated that we should be acquiring freezer trawlers now.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the fishery development plan prepared by the Atlantic provinces warned that, unless our fishing industry is rapidly developed, a large part of the potential economic benefits from our 200-mile zone will be unnecessarily deferred and possibly lost to Canada while foreign nations will continue to reap significant benefits.
With clearcut, long-term policies in place, developed in consultation with the industry, and which recognize the separation of government and industry roles, I feel certain the Canadian fishing industry can realize its potential both in economic and social terms. However, the time to act is now. For all these reasons I am pleased to support the amendment as moved by my leader.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne because I have a very deep concern about certain trends, certain ideas that are abroad in this land, and I think that there is a message that some of us are duty bound to give to this House. Someone has already said that we live in a time of paradox. On the one hand Canada is a wealthy country, our people are tremendous and the things that are around to make life good in this country are many, but, yet our time is marred by despair and fear. One wonders how we can be so afraid, living as we do in such a wonderful country.
I suspect that the despair and the fear relate, not so much to present conditions, but to the future. There is concern as to whether the good things that we have will continue or whether we may run into some kind of downturn that would make life in Canada less enjoyable than it is today. Having said that there are good things about life in Canada today, I want to say something about how those good things were achieved. I realize that I must be careful not to make myself out to be any older than I am, but I am 70 years of age. I have seen a good part of this century that Sir Wilfrid Faurier said would belong to Canada, and in many ways that prophecy has come true.
I also belong to the generation of Canadians that came of age, that started to get active in life generally and in public affairs in particular just as the depression of the 1930s was beginning. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) likes to refer to some of us as "leftovers from the depression", but I suggest that those of us who remember those days have a message that we must give. The thing I remember most about the thirties; perhaps even more than the suffering, the unemployment, the hunger and the poverty, was the consensus among our people that cut across party lines and religious lines; people in all kinds of organizations and groups were not only horrified by what we experienced in that decade of depression but were determined to bring such conditions to an end. We were determined that it must not happen again.
As a member of a political party I am prepared to state the role that my party played in those years and in the years that have transpired since; but if I may speak more objectively and more historically, I am happy to say that that generation that was alive and active in the 1930s was a generation with a

October 13, 1978

determination that was implemented in legislation to make Canada a better country. The characteristic of social and economic life of that period, the 1920s and the 1930s, was a minimum of government concern, a minimum of government intervention in the economy, and a minimum of government services. What we who belonged to the generation that got started in that decade were determined to do was to get the government into the economy and to provide services that private enterprise was not providing, and to establish social programs that would end forever the day when people would starve and die because they could not afford medical attention, or be impoverished in their old age.
I pay tribute to those who were older when I was just moving into the 1930s and to all who were part of that generation, that we stuck with it and achieved the things that we knew had to be achieved to make Canada the good country that it is today. The government got into things. It established legislation respecting labour relations, trade, industry, and many other things. It got more heavily into transportation- land, sea and air; it got into the activity of the Canadian Wheat Board and the marketing of other agricultural products; it got into housing; it got into the building of highways; it got into education by means of assistance to the provinces and by means of grants to enable people to take special courses; it got into social security in terms of old age pensions, family allowance and unemployment insurance and then, finally, as the crowning achievement of all, it got into hospitalization and health care.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that one of the reasons we can say that today life in Canada is good is because of these things that were fought for by the people of the generation to which I am happy to belong.
As I have already said, I could put this into political terms and talk about the parties and their particular role in achieving these things. But that really does not matter; what does matter is that a generation that knew what it was like to have a society in which there was non-intervention by the government, a society in which there was that lack of social services and lack of social programs-that generation saw to it that all of that was changed.
