speechtext:
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the deep concern to which I referred in my opening sentence is over the fact that there seems to be abroad in Canada today the notion that the government must get out of the economy, the notion that we must cut back, the notion that there must be restraint, and the notion that we have gone too far in terms of public services and social programs.
In the last two or three days I have heard on both sides of the House the word "privatizing" as though it is a sacred word or a new idea. Mr. Speaker, it is not new; it is as old as the poverty and suffering that some of us saw when we first became active in the life of this country.
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
I contend that if this country is going to make the mistake of turning back the clock, of going in for less government intervention in the economy and giving things back to private enterprise and the private sector, if the government is going to cut back on public services and refuse to continue to raise pensions and family allowances, or cut into programs for hospitalization and health care, a generation from now the government that took that backward step will be severely criticized. And rightly so!
I know that this hits both ways, Mr. Speaker. Certainly there is no doubt about my friends in the Progressive Conservative party. They want more to be left to the private sector. I heard a prominent Conservative talking outside the House the other day as though he were Adam Smith come back to life. He was saying that what was needed was more opportunity for great wealth to be made at the top so that more would trickle down to those at the bottom. That is a good Tory position. What bothers me today is that the government, the party that has the majority, is talking in those same terms, with two or three exceptions. There are two or three Liberals in the House who have their priorities straight, but for the most part the government today, and this House generally, seem to have forgotten the lesson some of us learned because we have seen several decades of life in this great country.
I call on this House not to fall for the notion that by privatizing services, by increasing unemployment through laying people off, by cutting out programs that the government has got into, by putting the lid on social programs, this will somehow get us on the right track. Mr. Speaker, that will put us back into conditions that may be quite satisfactory to corporation directors in the boardrooms of the nation, but they will make a serious difference so far as the ordinary people of this country are concerned.
That is what I like about what we have achieved in the last 40 or 50 years. People now count. I have stood in this House on previous occasions and told the story-something I shall never forget-of my younger days when I was a minister. I had the experience several times of going into the homes of people who were in my congregation and discovering older people, parents or grandparents, of whose existence I was not even aware. This was in the days when the pension was $20 a month and older people were kept somewhere in the backrooms. Often they just did not have the clothes to go out, and there was no life for them.
Over the years, by establishing the universal pension, by raising that amount, by lowering the age for receiving that pension and getting other pension improvements, by going in for senior citizens housing of various kinds, by getting universal hospitalization, health care and medical programs established, we have changed life completely for our older generation.
There is no comparison between what older people experienced 40 or 50 years ago and what they experience today. That has not come about by any privatization of things; that has not come about because we have left it to private enterprise and all that sort of nonsense. That came about

October 13, 1978
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
because the people of Canada, all of us through our collective institutions of government, saw to it that the economy was told to provide pensions and services and to make life better, not just for those who look at the balance sheets but to make life better for people themselves.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that far from speeches being made calling on us to get the government out, to privatize and so on, we should recognize we were right in the last 40 or 50 years- whatever party was in power-we were right in moving in the direction of more and more public concern, social concern, government concern for the economy and for what it does to our people. So, Mr. Speaker, that is why we have before the Elouse at this time the subamendment moved yesterday in the name of my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). It calls for the government to take steps to improve the employment situation and also-and this, I gather, is the phrase in the subamendment that turns off my friends in the Progressive Conservative party-it calls for a new program of public sector investment.
Maybe for a short while we shall be the voice crying in the wilderness, but it will not be long until it is recognized that we are right and that those who have followed this viewpoint for the last 30 or 40 years were right, especially on the Liberal side of the House. They were the ones who seemed to go that way the most, thanks to our prodding. What bothers me about the Liberals is that they are retreating from that position. They are talking about privatization, about curtailment; they are talking about more unemployment and uncertainty for the people so that they will appreciate what they have and get back on the track. That will not take us out of the difficulties we now face. Instead of doing that, we should do what is proposed in our amendment, take the economic steps to increase employment, and take steps to increase investment in the public sector.
Along with that I think this is the time when we should be improving our social services and social programs. If some of my colleagues have wondered if, in this speech in the address debate, I was not going to get to the subject of pensions, they now know there was never any intention of my not getting into that subject. Instead of talking about putting on means tests and giving only to those who supposedly need it and so on, we should be increasing the amount we pay as old age security. Let the income tax take it back, and let us make the changes in the income tax that are necessary for those who do not need the additional amount, but one way to make sure that more money will be spent on the purchase of consumer goods is to put more of it into the hands of our senior citizens.
Another way is to put more of that money into the hands of the families of this country. I quite approve of the part of the program having to do with children which provides an income tax credit of $200 a year per child to families whose incomes are below $18,000 a year, but I see no reason for cutting back the amount of the family allowance from its present $26 to $20 a month. It would be far better, Mr. Speaker, if that amount

were doubled. Put that money into the hands of the mothers of this country who need food and clothing for their children. The spending of the money will in itself have a beneficial effect on the economy of Canada.
So, I say, Mr. Speaker, this is not a time for cutting back on social programs; this is a time to be expanding those programs and to be confirming the judgment of four or five decades of parliamentarians who have sat in this place-that Canada is a better place in which to live because of what the government does. Therefore, this is not a time for the government to get out of our economy.
As I have already indicated, the amount of the old age pension should be increased, and not just for those who draw the guaranteed income supplement. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians, senior citizens, just over the line, who have just enough with their old age security and some other income not to qualify for the guaranteed income supplement. Because they do not qualify for the guaranteed income supplement, there are certain other benefits that they do not get, and they are having a rough time. I welcome the increase in the supplement to $20 a month. But as I say, there are hundreds of thousands of people just over the line, and the same is true with respect to family allowances. That is why across the board increases are so necessary.
While we are saying something about these benefits, particularly old age pensions, I think the argument that this is a time of restraint and that we have to cut back is no reason for not solving some serious problems that stand out in our pension program. I think the most unfair is what we do to single women who are between the ages of 60 and 65. That spouse's allowance, which is fine for those who get it, says to women between the ages of 60 and 65 who are spinsters, widows, divorced, or unattached in any way, that there is nothing for them. We go even further and say to the spouse who might be getting that allowance that because she is 62 or 63 and has a living husband, if he dies before she is 65 what she has is taken away from her. That is of a piece with other things in our pension program which are grossly unfair to the older women of this country. I want pensions improved across the board, but the more I study the situation, the more messages I get from people in trouble, the more I realize that the group which is most disadvantaged in their older years is our women, especially those women who are unattached because they are single or widowed.
This morning I was answering questions on one of those radio stations that call us sometimes from our constituencies. A woman had phoned in a question about her pension from the Canadian National Railways. It is the same whether the person is receiving a CNR pension, a public service pension, or what-have-you. Her husband had retired, gone on pension and died a month later. She discovered-she did not realize it would happen this way-that one month's full pension was paid in respect of her husband, but then for her it is cut in half. And yet, Mr. Speaker, as I had to say on the radio this morning to Winnipeg, if the reverse had happened, if she had died first, her husband's pension would have continued at 100
October 13, 1978

per cent. That applies to public service pensions and it applies to pensions of all kinds. Somehow or another it seems all right to continue the man's pension at its full amount, but we say to the woman, "You have to get by on 50 per cent or 60 per cent", or in some cases it is even less. That idea is for the birds. If pensions are defensible, as I say they are, if they are part of our structure, they should be there for our women on the same fair basis as they are for men.
I also made the point that pensions, generally speaking, should be put on a very firm and adequate basis so far as escalation is concerned. There are some who argue that the escalation is too much and want to cut it back. I point out that the escalation relates only to the rise in the cost of living, that in all plans it is already several months behind by the time a person gets it. It does not relate to the things pensioners have to buy. Actually we should be giving serious attention to putting our escalation of pensions on a basis that relates to our rising standard of living, one that relates to the increase in the gross national product.
These things do not appeal to those who draw up balance sheets and to those who sit in corporation board rooms. But that is not what this country is for. This country is for people, men, women and children, and it is for their benefit, just as by government intervention in the economy, by government programs, by social programs, we have made life better for our people over the years. We can make it still better in our time. We started these programs when the budget of the country was a great deal smaller than it is today. Of course, we were told then that these things could not be afforded, but we managed to afford them, and not only did we manage to afford them but life is better and the economy is better because we did so. So I call for increases in the old age pension, increases in family allowances and improvements in the escalation of all such programs.
I call upon the government to take steps to make sure that Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway pay decent pensions along the lines that have been recommended time and time again. I also call on the government to take steps to ensure that pensions in private industry are made subject to escalation even if it has to involve some kind of government addition to those pensions to make that possible.
I go back to my reference to the experience I had 30 or 40 years ago of finding, in homes I visited, older people of whose existence I was not aware. We have made life a lot better for them but we can make it a lot better still if we stay with the philosophy that has made this a good country, the philosophy of government concern-not the philosophy of government non-intervention which is being preached in this House day after day and which in itself means disaster down the road.
While mentioning pensions, and just in the minute or two before my time runs out, I want to say a special word about the pensions of veterans and their survivors. I think we have done well in the last few years in terms of winning improvements and getting the disability pension related to wage levels in the public service, getting those pensions up, getting prisoner of war compensation and so on. But there are still some
The Address-Mr. McRae
things which must be done. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) told us last session that the War Veterans Allowance Act was being reviewed and he hoped to have legislation brought in this fall. I trust that that will be done.
There still remains as an unfinished item the question of what happens to a widow of a disabled veteran if the disabled veteran's disability pension is below 48 per cent. Take the case of two widows. One was married to a veteran whose pension was 50 per cent; he died and she gets a full widow's pension. Next door is a widow whose husband when he died was on a 45 per cent pension; she gets no pension at all. It can be argued that she can qualify for the war veterans' allowance, or welfare measures of one kind or another, but why the distinction? Why do we carry it on all down the line? As the veterans who have survived World War II, let alone those from World War I, get older, they realize how important this is. They are calling for action to be taken on this issue of adequate pensions for their widows.
In that connection, may I just say, even if it is not quite related to the theme of my remarks this afternoon, that there is great concern among the veterans of this country over a case that happened a few weeks ago. A disabled veteran, an amputee, a man whose condition was very serious, such that he was getting a good deal of money from the Canadian Pension Commission, was denied the extra amount of money that was needed for the extra care that was required in his home. The day he got the notice that his request had been turned down, he died.
This has raised questions among veterans as to whether there needs to be a review of the terms and conditions under which disability pensions and the attachments thereto are awarded. I hope this will be done. As I said the other day, I think it was a mistake that there was no reference to veterans in the Speech from the Throne. Despite that, I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs will join with us in seeing that something is done, and that it is done very soon.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you are taking the position that you take when a member's time is about up. I will not make it necessary for you to tell me that my time is up. I am glad to have had this opportunity to speak again. As I say, I hope I have not sounded older than I am, speaking for my generation, the senior citizens of Canada today who did something tremendous for this country. The country owes them a lot for resolving to build back in the thirties the kind of country in which the government would care. I plead for that to be continued. It is on that basis that I call for support for our plea for increases in our social programs, and for support this afternoon when the vote comes on our amendment to the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this

October 13, 1978
The Address-Mr. McRae
debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne and to echo some of the concerns expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
We must be extremely concerned about those in our society who are having a tough time getting along because this is a very rich society. I certainly agree with many of the concerns the hon. member expressed about pensions. There are many who are just marginally getting along, although with a great deal of difficulty.
The philosophy espoused by the hon. member is one that I accepted for many years, the idea that the state can do everything. However, I have changed my views a great deal. In recalling the thirties, forties and fifties, the hon. member recalled the need for the kinds of solutions he mentioned. However, he should understand there are massive changes occuring at the present time. These changes mean we have to move in different directions.
The solutions which he outlined are solutions that I accepted in the fifties and sixties but which do not at this point pertain. We must understand that we are in a new economic age. Once we understand that, we can begin to take steps to cope with it.
It is particularly disturbing at this point in our history that parties like the New Democratic Party, which have shown the way for so long, should be dealing with problems of the fifties and sixties and not the problems of our present time. There are three essential factors which are responsible for this great change in global economic thinking. This change has not occurred to a lot of economists' thinking, but should occur.
First, there has been a quantum jump in the problems that face all governments. For the past 100 years this country and other nations could expect inflation rates in the order of 1 per cent or 2 per cent, perhaps even less. Today, when our Prime M inister (Mr. Trudeau) attends a meeting of the big seven or our Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) attends a meeting of the IMF, they look at 5 per cent as being a zero point. It is from plus or minus zero after five that they start working. This is a totally new concept globally. There have been high inflation rates for short periods of time in some countries, but 5 per cent plus has not been a global phenomenon in the past.
Unemployment problems are rising in all parts of the world. The past ten years has been a period of very substantial growth. That is now changing and we are getting growth rates of 2 per cent or 3 per cent per annum. We see a rise in social problems in most communities throughout the world. We see a significant change in the policy of governments to cope with currency problems. This is because the nation state no longer has the power it used to have given the fact that so much of our liquid assets are controlled by global or multinational corporations. This whole series of events in the past six or seven years has been summed up in this quantum leap in the problems that face all nations.
The second factor is the introduction of an almost totally unique phenomenon, scarcity. I was taught to believe that was something bankers or some other group dreamed up, and that

if we could only get rid of that notion we could solve all problems.
For the first time in the history of mankind we are facing a real scarcity, possibly not in the immediate future, but certainly in the next ten to 15 years. I refer, of course, to shortage of energy. Already the energy problem has created some massive economic problems. This is one of the reasons for the present state of the American dollar; the American economy has a very large deficit in its oil account. I believe last year it was in the order of $45 billion to $50 billion. This is a flow of money from the United States to the Arab states and the OPEC countries. We face the same problem, although not to the same degree.
There are other problems along that line which we face. We have been told that in the next 15 years we will need approximately $180 billion of capital for energy projects, that the percentage of our capital expenditures that go into energy will increase from 10 per cent to between 30 per cent and 40 per cent. That is a unique factor, something we will hear a great deal more of as time goes on.
The third factor in terms of a new economic thinking is that techniques used in the past no longer obtain. They do not work the way they used to. There are two reasons for this. First, the magnitude of the problem makes it impossible to use monetary or fiscal techniques to solve it. Second, the Keynesian techniques, both monetary and fiscal, tend at this point to be counter-productive. It was always a theory that if one increased the amount of money that goes into people's pockets, this would create jobs. However, where you have a situation of high inflation and high unemployment, a parallel situation, very often increases in demand will increase inflation, increase unit costs, decrease sales abroad as well as locally, and possibly result in more unemployment.
I give that one example to show that measures considered effective in the past do not work in today's conditions. It is important we should realize when looking at the problems of our time, especially when we are facing an election, that one cannot come up with old solutions and expect good things to happen. This applies particularly to spokesmen for opposition parties. I do not think one can come up with old solutions and expect Canadians to accept them.
Dealing specifically with the Canadian scene, I should like to outline two or three of the major problems we face and, possibly, suggest some solutions. I shall speak, first of all, of unemployment, because in my view unemployment is at the heart of our difficulties as a country. There are certain features which are unique to this country, features which do not obtain in other countries, and for this reason many of the actions the government has been obliged to take and which tend to disturb the economy have been taken because of the constraints of unemployment.
If we assume 1965 to be the base year and equate the number of people available for employment in each of the major countries in that year to 100, we find that for every 100
October 13, 1978

people in the labour force in West Germany in 1965 there are 96 in the labour force today. For every 100 in the labour force in the United Kingdom in 1965 there are today 103 or 104. In Italy the figure is around 100, in France it is 110, in Sweden 112 and in Japan, 114. The figure in all of these countries is between 96 and 114, so that in most of them the increase amounts to six or seven per hundred compared with the figure 12 years ago.
Three countries are rather different, however. One of them is the United States, where there were 28 more people per hundred in the labour force at the end of 1977 than there were in 1965. In Australia there were 30 more people in the labour force. Now, when we turn to Canada we find that Canada is in an entirely unique position, the labour force having grown from 100 to 146 on the basis I have outlined. In other words, over that 12-year period no other country has shown this astonishing increase.
Now, Mr. Speaker, even on the basis of an 8.5 per cent rate of unemployment, or 9 per cent as New Democratic spokesmen tend to assert, we would still have a shortage of people to do jobs if we had done just as well as the United States in creating jobs.
This situation has caused great concern and difficulty for industry in the private sector and for governments at federal and provincial levels. First, the cost of our massive unemployment insurance scheme is running at between $4 billion and $5 billion-something we would not need were it not for the rapid growth in the labour force to which I have referred.
Moreover, massive amounts of expenditure are involved in DREE, in internal payments to provinces, in the Canada Works program and in various incentive programs designed to create jobs. All these expenditures are connected to the one dominant problem I have mentioned.
I find myself terribly disturbed that these facts are not better known to Canadians generally, because it is only when we understand them that we can do something about them. It is certain that the deficit on the national account is dictated largely by this single question of unemployment. I would estimate that in round terms our $11.5 billion deficit would disappear were it not for unemployment, and were it not for the massive rise in the labour force.
I should like to deal briefly, now, with some of the other problems we are facing. I refer to inflation. We are all to blame in one way or another for what has happened. We could expect a normal inflation rate of 1 per cent or 2 per cent over the years but, as hon. members know, it is running at between 7 per cent and 9 per cent, likely in the order of 7.5 per cent this year. Most other countries are in a similar situation; anyone who has travelled outside Canada and the United States will certainly be aware of that. While we are experiencing a higher inflation rate in Canada than, say, in Switzerland, the cost of everything in Switzerland is much higher in real terms than in Canada.
I believe that over the years the government has made a real effort to lower the inflation rate. When wage settlements were
The Address-Mr. McRae
running around 22 per cent in 1975, we thought it necessary to impose controls and we did, against the advice of a great many people and in spite of the concern expressed by some spokesmen for the labour movement. The result was that in two or three years we were able to reduce those increases to something in the order of 7 per cent. As a matter of fact, the increase in the cost of labour in this country is running at a considerably lower rate today than it is in the United States; the unit labour cost in the U.S. went up by 6.4 per cent last year while in Canada the increase was only 5.6 per cent. So we have had some luck, or we have been effective, perhaps I should say, in reducing our inflation rate and bringing it down to a figure which is at least equivalent to that of some our friends and neighbours.
The continuance of inflation is the one single problem over which the economists I speak to worry most in terms of the possibility of a world recession. They are particularly concerned about what is happening in the United States where the rate of inflation is rising sharply at this moment. If the situation gets out of hand we might very well face a major depression as a result.
Another area I wish to deal with concerns government spending. The government has been accused for many years of spending money outrageously and many hold the opinion that most of this country's problems, including inflation and the weakness of the Canadian dollar, are directly attributable to government spending. In particular, they blame the federal government. This is not necessarily the case, of course.
It is important to understand the way in which government spending is distributed. In other words, who benefits from the money which the federal government collects? The major expenditure is, of course, on transfer payments.
Because of inflation and all kinds of other reasons, we transferred 52.3 per cent of government expenditures in the form of pensions and family allowances and in the form of various subsidies to other levels of government.
The next item has to do with the government debt which costs in the neighbourhood of 15.8 per cent. Then there are some payments to Crown corporations, costing 3.3 per cent, which gives us a total of 71.4 per cent of all the money that the federal government spends in transfer payments, on the public debt and money which goes to Crown corporations to keep them in operation. The rest of the money, which amounts to only 28 per cent, runs the whole operation of the government.
So when the opposition, particularly the Tory opposition, refer to government cuts, they are talking about this 28.6 per cent. Because I do not think they dare go very far into the other areas. I do not know how you can get these kinds of cuts out of 28 per cent. Sure, there are some things we can do, but it is difficult to say that we can cut massive sums out of government spending unless we go into the transfer area or unless we take it out of people's pensions or out of the money that goes to the provinces.

October 13, 1978
The Address-Mr. McRae
The other thing of which we are accused is that we are that part of the government which grows the fastest. In other words, all the problems are caused by the federal government.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I should like to indicate that since 1961 the federal government's portion of the GNP has risen from 18.1 per cent to 20.2 per cent; in other words, roughly an increase of 10 per cent. We bit into more of it than we did in the past for many reasons. However, the provinces' and municipalities' share has gone up from 12.7 per cent to 20.1 per cent, roughly a 70 per cent increase. The other levels of government have increased their expenditures at seven times the rate we have. So let us not ascribe all the difficulties to the federal government, as the Tories in particular would want to do.
The other point I would like to mention about government revenues, and this is of great concern, is the large deficit we have at present. I would like to indicate one of the reasons why this deficit is growing at such a rapid rate. If one looks at the chart showing the expenditures of the government alongside government revenues, one sees that the two lines run parallel and are very close together going all the way back to 1970 and through 1974. But all of a sudden, about the end of 1974, the revenue starts to decline.
I think that if we are looking at the reasons for the deficit we look for the reason for that decline, why the revenue has fallen off. There are many factors, but I would say that one of them was that when we were indexing family allowances and pensions we also indexed taxation in the sense that the tax break, the money people got back in allowances and so on, was indexed so that each individual was able to claim a larger break in the taxation area. Of course, this resulted in an increased deficit. I recall the time in 1974 when we were bringing down the budget which brought this provision in, Mr. Turner's budget. The real push for this came from the Tory opposition during the minority parliament.
Those are just a few thoughts 1 have on government expenditures. I agree that for many reasons we have to cut back and operate more efficiently than we have; but I also think that Canadians should understand that it will be very difficult to make effective cuts in government spending because we control less than one third of what the government spends. The actual expenditures, 70 per cent of them, are going to transfers, over many of which the government has little control because they are legislated.
The last point I want to mention, and I will do it very briefly, has to do with the Canadian dollar. From discussions 1 have had with many economists and from my own research 1 have come to the conclusion that the Canadian dollar is seriously undervalued at present, especially in view of the fact that in the last several months manufacturing capacity in this country has increased from 81 per cent to close to 86.5 per cent. We have had a slow but steady growth in our manufacturing capacity. We have had a much slower growth in the cost of labour than have some other countries, and our productivity has increased in comparison with other countries.

I think that for this and for many other reasons the Canadian dollar will tend to seek a higher level over the next short period. In the meantime, this fall has been a definite advantage to some Canadians, and I can cite two reasons. One is an increase-in spite of what the previous Tory speaker said-in the level of our exports to other countries simply because, by having a lower dollar, our exports have become more competitive. Another factor which has affected this increase in capacity in terms of our manufacturing industry is that our Canadian producers, producing for the home market are in a much more favourable position and are able to compete better with the higher cost imports. This is a factor which tells me that our trade balance has improved fairly rapidly. Because of the effect of these two factors on our trade balance, we will find that the dollar will improve its position over the next several months.
Finally, 1 should like to deal with some of the solutions that I hear offered by members of the opposition, i am concerned, particularly in the context of my introductory remarks, about the approach that the opposition parties, and sometimes some of our members on this side, are taking to these problems. If we assume we are in a period of new economics, if we assume, for instance, as Mr. Callaghan said, that we cannot buy our way out of this, then why are we concentrating on these kinds of approaches like the Tory approach of a couple of billion dollars in tax savings in the area of mortgages and other taxes? This is done partly to give some relief to the taxpayers, but it is mostly done in the name of creating jobs. We seem to assume that by cutting back a couple of billion dollars and increasing the deficit, all of a sudden we will start creating jobs.
Anyone who has any understanding of the new economic thinking or of what is happening in our times realizes that this kind of action does not have this effect. I do not care whether it is our own finance people or people on the other side to whom I am talking. I am saying that in the new economic era a couple of billion dollars will not make any difference, partly because we have a level of savings which is five times what it was in the early 1960s. Approximately 10 per cent of the GNP goes into savings, as opposed to a little over 2 per cent in the sixties.
The other thing we should remember when we talk about saving a couple of billion dollars is that we used to talk about that figure in the sixties-just throw another couple of billion dollars in to stimulate the economy. That was at a time when the G.N.P. was approximately $50 billion. Now we are talking about $220 billion and something less than 1 per cent as a stimulant. We should begin to understand the kinds of changes which are occurring in our economic systems. For instance, for the benefit of the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party, Keynes is dead. Keynes is finished in terms of any serious movement toward changes in economic positions. We should start to look at a new way of approaching the thing. The problems have changed. The techniques we used in the past do not work today. When we realize that, we will stop seeing the
October 13, 1978

answers as a simplistic increasing of the deficit by another couple of billion dollars.
All governments are facing much more serious problems than ever before. We have the notion of scarcity which was not there before. Keynesian techniques which have been so convenient over the last 35 or 40 years just do not work. We must look for different answers if we are even marginally to correct the problems which face us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I am pleased to be able to take part in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. However, I am saddened after six years of participation in these debates that matters have not changed very much. In fact, there is a sense that one has heard it all before.
When I witnessed the Speech from the Throne as a new member of parliament some six years ago, I was impressed and excited with the multitude of promises made and the many words exulting success and hope for Canada and Canadians in every field and walk of life. Unfortunately my naive glimmer of expectation at that time was short-lived. My hopes were shattered when I quickly realized that this administration was outlining in the Speech from the Throne a series of hollow words and false expectations of which very few, if any, would materialize.
The Speech from the Throne six years ago was not an isolated incident. One can simply look at the record of subsequent speeches, many budgets and many Liberal campaign promises, such as we are faced with right now, and conclude that time after time the present government has not lived up to its promises. It continues to make them and it continues to break them to the point of misleading the public.
Of course, we do not have to go back six years for examples. I am sure all hon. members and all Canadians will recall the 1974 election campaign when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) shouted and yelled at the top of his voice that income and price controls would never be implemented in this country. At that time we proposed a 90-day price freeze in order to establish a positive and realistic economic policy. We all know what happened as soon as the Prime Minister received his mandate. He slapped wage and price controls on Canadians far more stringent than those proposed by my party. That is but just one example. There are many, many others too numerous to mention at this time in view of our time limitations. It is because of this continuing attitude that our country is deteriorating from what was once a healthy, unified, free enterprise nation to the divided, socialist-stricken state which I believe exists today.
Turning to a more personal note, I came to Canada in 1949 as a child, having left a depressed nation where the freedoms of speech, hope, opportunity and enterprise were snuffed out by a government dedicated to socialism. I came to Canada with my family, along with many new Canadians, because Canada was a young, vibrant, growing country offering opportunity, hope, diversification and freedom of all kinds, including that of enterprise. Included in this bountiful and beautiful
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
country were governments which offered a work ethic atmosphere that was the envy of nations around the world. They were governments which offered an incentive to its peoples and industries and rewarded them accordingly.
At that time Canadians were proud of a hard day's work, and new Canadians were honoured to come to this country in order to join that work force. Canada grew and prospered in a united front. In the last decade, a decade which has been governed by our present Prime Minister, unfortunately this trend has reversed itself. Government incentives have disappeared, only to be replaced by handouts and give-aways. Frustration has taken over from pride. Hope and opportunity have been replaced by confusion and despair.
Yet there is no reason why our country cannot be the leader in the industrialized world. As we all know, Canada is the wealthiest nation per capita as far as natural resoures are concerned. Our human resource is surpassed by none. Our technological know-how is the best in the world. Yet our country is falling apart. Our productivity is at its lowest level in years. Unemployment and inflation rates are far too high and climbing. I will not refer to the figures at this point because they are common knowledge. Our currency has lost the confidence of international money makers and of Canadians as well. Canadians have stopped investing in Canada because the incentive is not here. Even the government has lost confidence in our dollar. One of its agencies, Loto Canada, whether inadvertently or not, decided to give away gold as its million dollar prize rather than the Canadian dollar.

Everyone knows he is no longer "Joe Who", Mr. Speaker, but rather the Leader of the Opposition. Instead of reiterating those proposals our leader has been making for some time, I should like to dwell briefly on that area of my responsibility on behalf of this party, namely, the area of small business.
As hon. members know, this vital sector of our economy is responsible for the employment of roughly 60 per cent of the labour force and, therefore, is a sector that can make or break the economic fabric of our nation. In view of the continual disturbance throughout my remarks caused by the NDP, perhaps 1 should suggest that they would like to nationalize even the small businesses of this nation.
Although the Prime Minister did appoint a member of his cabinet over two years ago to look after the affairs of the small businessman in Canada, and this at our urging, the fact remains that this sector continues to be sadly overlooked. It was the initiative of the Conservative party that prompted the first full debate on small business in parliament on March 28, 1977. We have had the opportunity to repeat that debate on
October 13, 1978

several occasions since, each time outlining in detail the many specific recommendations beneficial not only to the small business community but to our economy as a whole.
It is true, of course, that as a result of our insistence, as well as the urging of such small business interest groups as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, chambers of commerce and others, the government was shamed into taking some belated steps in the proper direction. Unfortunately, with each little step the government has taken forward in respect of small business it has taken a giant step backwards in general economic matters.
It is not just specific small business policies that affect small business, as I hope to outline quickly in just a few moments; it is also the lack of general long-range programs that adversely affect the over-all economy of Canada. One example is this government's inability to act decisively in respect of labour situations. Instead of trying to unite labour and management with government, it creates a spirit of confrontation. Each time Canadians are threatened by an essential service strike, which unfortunately is regularly, the government panics and ends up by legislating the strikers back to work. Unfortunately, the economy suffers and Canadians are inconvenienced. In addition, when you legislate an essential service union back to work you in fact take away the right to strike.
We all know we are once again faced with a postal strike. I refer again to this matter because such a strike has an adverse effect on everyone, but on no one more than the small businessman. The small businessman depends on daily mail delivery. Postal strikes have been regular in this country as a result of the inability of this government to establish some long-range policy. Small businesses have suffered drastically, to the extent that every time there is a postal strike many small businesses go bankrupt. This adds to our unemployment situation, to our poor productivity and our inflation, not to mention the millions of dollars lost to our economy and the inconvenience caused to all Canadians.
Indeed, it was a surprise last August 1 when the Prime Minister went on television without telling anybody in his cabinet, in the civil service or anywhere else, and said that he was finally fed up with what was going on within the Post Office. He must have been the last Canadian to be fed up with the post office situation; I do not know where he has been for the last few years. That was August 1 and since then he has not done one thing about it. Already we have had one rotation of strikes and now we are on the eve of having a national strike once again, after the Prime Minister finally decided that he was fed up with the Post Office situation.
The Post Office is not only to blame for this matter, because it is a fact that the government has no long-range, realistic policies in that regard, that there is trouble within the Post Office, and, indeed, within the civil service and the whole labour situation throughout Canada.
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
Our party back on May 18, 1977, was concerned to such a point with the Post Office situation that we used one of our opposition days to discuss it. I will read the motion from that day under the name of my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). It reads as follows:
That this House notes with alarm the government's continuing inability to provide Canadians with an efficient postal service, its obsession with secrecy, its illegal use of orders in council to set postal rates, and its chronic ineptness in the field of collective bargaining and industrial relations, and recommends that the operations of the Post Office Department be referred to a special joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate.
That was in May of last year, a year and a half ago. It was a good recommendation that received good debate from everybody. Yet for a year and a half the government have sat on their rumps without taking one positive step to deal with the situation; hence we are stuck with a forthcoming postal strike.
Two days ago I took the opportunity to move a motion under Standing Order 43 similar to this motion made by the hon. member pleading with this House to form a joint committee to study the proposals and recommendations that have come forward and to deal with the matter once and for all, rather than dealing with the Post Office on an ad hoc basis. Again it was rejected by the government because they would rather wait until the country was hit with a postal strike and with the disruption it causes the country, the small businessman and every industry from coast to coast. My recommendation falls along the same lines of that of my colleague from Brandon-Souris. 1 would like to see that committee formed, a joint committee of members from the House of Commons and the Senate.
What would that committee study, Mr. Speaker? Recommendations from many people. Very quickly, my recommendations would be as follows. First, we should study within that committee the possibility of sector bargaining. I have a secret cabinet memo of two years ago where this was discussed in cabinet after the government was questioned on sector bargaining. It makes so much sense because each industry within our economy has three, four, five or more different unions within it. The Post Office is no different. The letter carriers went on a rotating strike last month. That issue was settled and now we have CUPW going on strike.
Another example is the airlines. First we had the pilots threatening to strike. That issue was settled after a lot of money was spent on negotiations. The airlines went back into operation and then it was the baggage handlers who struck. I am not sure if I have it in the right order. After the baggage handlers it was the stewards and stewardesses. Next will be someone else, another union within the airlines. There are too many unions within each industry. It would be far simpler and make more sense to deal with each sector as one unit and in that way at least Canadians would be free of strikes in essential service sectors for the duration of the contract.
Talking about the strike, I am sorry to report to the hon. members present that on the four o'clock radio news, ten minutes ago, Mr. Parrot of CUPW walked out of the talks that were in progress. This is the attitude we get. There is no

October 13, 1978
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
doubt in my mind, now that Mr. Parrot has walked out, that we will be in a strike situation. I will support back to work legislation as soon as it is presented to us, but that is not the solution for the future and neither is the proposal of making the Post Office a Crown corporation. Air Canada is a Crown corporation. What is the government trying to do before an election? It is trying to fool the people into thinking that if the Post Office is made a Crown corporation, the situation will be resolved. There is no way that can happen.
Another area that I would like to see studied in committee is secret ballot voting. Hon. members will recall that last year the postal strike in Toronto took place because the majority of the rank and file members in the Toronto union did not get a chance to vote, and when they did vote they were afraid to go against the self-proclaimed radical leaders within that union. And they were self-proclaimed; it was public knowledge.
If the union is not afraid to follow the wishes of its rank and file members, they should not be opposed to secret ballot voting within the unit. For that matter, if the unions were not afraid of dealing directly and positively with the situation, I do not think that they should be afraid of a government-appointed overseer within the unions so that baseball bat tactics would be eliminated. I am not making things up when I say this because we all know that this is the case with many of our militant unions, whether it be the seafarers union or others.
Our party has been prompting the government to create such a committee instead of dealing on an ad hoc basis and saying, "Oh, yes, we are going to legislate them back to work." I would like to speak longer on this subject, but 1 said that I would move to different matters, and I know that my time is running out.
Briefly, I would like to refer to our small business policy. As the Leader of the Opposition said, "We don't mind the government stealing our policies as long as it is for the well-being of the country." Certainly the small businessman needs to be looked after. We would recommend two things to help small business. First, we recommend the removal of as much government regulation, directives and controls from small business as possible. Let small businesses operate on their own. The minister must be commended for finally taking steps to reduce the paperwork burden.
This is a small step in the right direction, but it does not go far enough. Our party would create, and it will create after the next election, a small business secretariat which is independently operated through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott), sincere as he may be, with the small business community, has his hands tied behind his back in trying to deal with the problems and potential of small business because he has to go through the massive bureaucracy of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, which is run by the old cowboy-who will no longer be here after the next election.
Under this independent secretariat we would pass a small business act which would, first of all, define what small

business is. Ironic as it may seem this government does not yet know what the definition of small business is. We have asked time and time again and each time they have given a different definition. This confuses small businessmen in the country even more than they are already because they do not know into which category they fall.
Third, we would pass a small business act which would encompass the over-all problems of the small business sector and create such incentives and policies as tax incentives for investment in small business, the creation of an export and import consortium operated through the government and assisted by the government, a "set aside" program that made sure that a certain portion of products, management and so on, would be purchased by governments rather than just big business. I will not go over our whole policy again as we have stated it on many other occasions.
I should like to close by reading one editorial, if I may, Mr. Speaker. I am not one for reading editorials but I think this one sums up the wastefulness of this government-the wastefulness of borrowing money and lending to other countries and the fact that we are not taking care of ourselves before we take care of others.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to seize this opportunity to talk about my area, eastern Quebec. It is my sincere belief, Mr. Speaker, that if Canada were to experience today the intense problems facing the Gaspe peninsula we would have an open revolution on our hands. You have no idea of the degree of suffering and misery to be found in that area which I am proud to have represented for the past ten years. And if you allow me, I would like to begin by quoting some figures on this all at once so beautiful and so battered area which hardly represents 1 per cent of the Canadian population. But the better to show the acuity of the problems plaguing that area I will put them into perspective with those of the province of Quebec.
From 1961 to 1971, the population of Quebec has increased by 14.6 per cent while at the same time the population of the Gaspe peninsula, more precisely that of the Lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe peninsula has experienced a decrease of 6.8 per cent. These figures would take a more dramatic significance if I mentioned that the Gaspe peninsula is the only area of Quebec which has had a decline in its population over the past 15 years. All areas of Quebec have had an increase in their population and in four of these areas-As everyone knows, Quebec is divided into ten administrative regions and once again only the Gaspe peninsula has experienced a drop in
October 13, 1978

its population during the past 15 years. As for the other regions, four have experienced an increase in their population above the average rate for Quebec and they are the Montreal area, the Outaouais region, the city of Quebec and the North Shore. It is also the Gaspe peninsula which has had such a negative balance in migratory trends that it has offset its natural increase. As a matter of fact nearly 140,000 people have left eastern Quebec since 1961.
It is also the most rural area in Quebec with the majority of its people, 53 per cent, being considered rural people. Furthermore, we have barely 4 per cent of Quebec's labour force. To further illustrate how our area is shrinking I will mention that the number of people working in 1961 was higher than the number working at the time of the last census in 1971. In fact the number of people who had a job decreased by 1.3 per cent. Indeed, in 1961 there were 84,267 people working as against 83,150 in 1971. It is the only area in Quebec to have experienced such a drop. I remind you, to put those figures in a national perspective, that every year in Canada we have 250,000 more people working than the previous year while in my area, even in absolute figures, there are fewer people working today than 15 years ago.
On the other hand, if we look at the participation rate, that is the relationship between the labour force and the total population 18 years of age and over, we see that in the Gaspe area the rate is the lowest in the province with 45.6 per cent while in Quebec it is 52 per cent. In other words we consider a good part of the people in the Gaspe area as part of the labour force while we all know that if work were available there would be no reason why we should have a lower participation rate than the national average.
However it is the less educated area not because people do not go to school but quite the contrary because every year about 7,000 youths as soon as they are out of the Polyvalente or the CEGEP leave the area because of a lack of work. It is also the area where the average income per worker is the lowest in Quebec. According to the latest statistics of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, incomes were about 60 per cent lower than in the Montreal metropolitan area.
As concerns unemployment, I find it most surprising and discouraging that while we have the lowest activity and participation level in the province of Quebec we also have the highest unemployment rate. I shall quote a letter dated September 23, 1974 from the then minister of manpower and immigration, the hon. Mr. Andras, now President of the Treasury Board, who wrote me:
As you mentioned, there is no doubt that the general unemployment level in Gaspe is higher than in Newfoundland.
So, as concerns our unemployment rate it is the highest in the province of Quebec and I would even say in Canada.
The Address-Mr. De Bane
Contrarily to the province of Quebec as a whole, unemployment is higher in the male population to the extent that the male labour fore has decreased between 1961 and 1971 in spite of an increase in the male population 15 years old or more. According to the statistics bureau of the government of Quebec, personal income in the province has soared by 130 per cent between 1961 and 1971. If you do not take Montreal centre into account, it rose during that decade by 160 per cent for the whole province and by 124 per cent for Gaspe. So, even in light of those figures which are somewhat less dramatic than the first I quoted, you see that the gap is still widening.
On the other hand, the per capita personal income is the lowest in Quebec. Indeed, it should be noted that this area has the lowest rate of activity and the highest average family size. What is even more surprising, Mr. Speaker, is that transfer payments represent 22 per cent of personal income, and this is where we have the highest per capita percentage. It is not in our area that transfer payments are the highest. In our area, in eastern Quebec, they are $405 per capita while they amount to $464 per capita in the eastern townships, for example. There are many reasons for this. For instance, unemployment insurance is based on the wages earned during the employment period and other such factors.
I mentioned earlier certain population shifts. The population of eastern Quebec was at its highest in 1961 with 349,000 people, but since then it has been going down regularly to such a point that today, even with a very high birth rate, it reaches only about 318,000. Of course, the area has long been the victim of negative migration, but with the fall of the birth rate, there is no natural increase to compensate for these negative migration figures. Once again, the characteristic which I find most eloquent and most depressing is that the number of workers in the Gaspe peninsula is lower now than it was 15 years ago. In absolute numbers, there are 1,000 fewer workers today than in 1961. Yet, during that same period, we have created several million jos in Canada and, each year, the labour force increases by over 250,000 people. Some will say to this that the answer for an area with as many resources as ours would be to rationalize the various resource sectors.
In this regard, the Economic Council of Canada recently published a remarkable study by Mr. Michel Boisvert on the correspondence between the urban system and the economic base of Canadian regions. This paper includes a study on eastern Quebec, and I must say that this effort of rationalization and consolidaton of basic and resource sectors of traditional sectors has been going on in the Gaspe area for a few years. However, I do not believe that we can hope to increase the number of jobs in these various sectors in the future for the simple reason that most of the effort and the progress have already been made. So, in forestry operations for instance, it is noted that on Crown lands, the coniferous forests west of the Matapedia Valley are developed to the extent of almost 100 per cent of their potential. In the eastern part of the region,

The Address-Mr. De Bane because of a more rugged topography, the potential is not fully developed. However, the development of coniferous forests on Crown lands is comparatively intensive. As far as private wood lots are concerned, conifers seem to be overexploited throughout the territory.
As regards farming, it seems that more than an economic acreage has been cleared up. Although farming on the coastal plain and along the Chaleur Bay is definitely profitable, several hinterland farms are switching to beef cattle production or are sold to city dwellers who leave them in fallow.
The area is not exempt either from the problem of getting young farmers to take over, rampant throughout Quebec. Marine fisheries went through a strong expansionary period in the early 1970s, but the level of catches has been declining since because of a significant decrease in resources. In mining, there is a marked slowdown in copper-related activities. Caused by unfavourable pricing conditions on the international scene, this slowdown has been mainly featured by the closing down of the Madeleine mines and also by declining activities in Murdochville.
In the tourist industry, the yearly volume of clients varies between 350,000 and 500,000, and apparently that level is difficult to exceed. All this suggests, Mr. Speaker, that the traditional ways of managing resources in eastern Quebec may have reached their maximum potential. The exploitation of resources leaves little room for additional job creation and limits expansion in the manufacturing industry. Barring changes, unemployment will remain high, emigration will continue and the population will decline. This tendency toward an extensive use of economic resources is coupled with another factor of equal significance to our area, namely the specialization of productions. The agricultural effort was directed mainly towards dairy production. Forestry went progressively towards pulp and paper, while our mineral production is still strongly concentrated on copper.
But this specialization in production leads necessarily to dependency. This dependency is particularly felt on our regional economy which is very sensitive to any change in government policies and to international market fluctuations. For example lower copper prices on world markets forced closure of the Madeleine mines. The entire agricultural sector is being affected by changes made in dairy policies and in policies on feed grain movements. The future of the forestry industry will have to be revised in light of tighter international competition for the production of pulp and paper and in view of the higher cost of imported energy.
Finally, a generally unfavourable economic context directly influences tourism. This phenomenon of specialization makes the economy of the region even more vulnerable, all the more so when the exploitation of its resources is already close to its maximum. And what is more remarkable, Mr. Speaker, is that

these efforts of normalization still brought a decrease in labour or a rise in skilled labour but over-all it meant a smaller labour force.
For example in 1971 agriculture, forestry, fisheries and mines accounted for 17 per cent of skilled labour in the area and for 13.2 per cent of the gross domestic products at factor cost. For the whole of Quebec, this ratio was 5.6 per cent and 6.2 per cent. Nevertheless between 1961 and 1971, the effects of serious strengthening of our primary industry and of the development of secondary and tertiary industries were being felt and the economy of eastern Quebec was undergoing substantial strutural change. In 1961, 30 per cent of the skill employed in the area and 20 per cent of the gross domestic product were corrected to primary industry. In terms of labour, between 1961 and 1971, agriculture lost 52 per cent of its strength, forestry 66 per cent and fishery 23.7 per cent. Mines were the only industry with a growth of 5.6 per cent between April 1961 and 1971. To conclude these statistics on the region, Mr. Speaker, eastern Quebec is still the area with the lowest employment rate and the highest unemployment rate in Quebec.
In 1971, only 45 per cent of all men and women over 15 were in the labour force. For Quebec as a whole, I repeat that this percentage was 52.9 per cent. Moreover, that year, some 5,300 eastern Quebec residents, that is 6.3 per cent of the active labour force, were working outside the province. In spite of this, 16 per cent of the labour force was unemployed in June. Unemployment statistics also show clearly the importance of seasonal activities: agriculture, fishing, forestry, peat bogs, tourism.
One notes a sharp difference between June and October, when the unemployment rate goes from 13 per cent to 17 per cent, and betwen November and May, when it goes from 20 per cent to 26 per cent. No other region shows such sharp fluctuations. For Quebec as a whole, the gap between the best summer month and the worse winter month is less than 2 per cent. On the other hand, considering government investments per capita, one realizes that they were less than the Quebec average for 1976-77.
Mr. Speaker, after having drawn such a picture, I think the conclusion is quite clear: new means of action will be required. In the last ten years or so, since 1968 to be more precise, the federal and Quebec governments have invested together $411 million to upgrade the various sectors in the Gaspe peninsula and equip that region with infrastructures. About S300 million out of those $411 million came from the federal government.
Unfortunatey, one finds today that despite the offer made several times to the Quebec government, the one now in power in that province, they still refuse to enter into another general agreement for eastern Quebec, even though under the first agreement the Quebec government was responsible for identifying, defining, developing and implementing the projects, while the federal government was paying almost three quarters
October 13, 1978

of the amount. Today they refuse to enter into another agreement and 1 think the federal government should, under the circumstances, amend the Department of Regional Economic Expansion Act in order to allow that department itself, within our own jurisdictio, to take action in this area by other means than sectorial agreements which have little impact on the area or again through industrial incentives.
So that is, in my view, my first recommendation. The second, Mr. Speaker, is that the Department of Finance should introduce fiscal measures giving the private sector such a marked advantage that it would compensate for the drawbacks inherent in establishing a business in such a remote area. There are only a few paths open to us, Mr. Speaker. Either we let the people continue to emigrate reluctantly from an area which does not alow them to earn a living, or the state becomes a providence state, an employer state, or else, as I just said, the Department of Finance should drop its uniform income tax schedule across the counry. For instance, if we were to tell businessmen considering the possibility of operating in such an area that they would not have to pay any income on profits for a period of ten or 25 years, provided the profits are reinvested in the area, I feel, I am convinced such a solution not only would cost the government less than the transfer payments we are making now, but also would give back a sense of dignity to the population.
I see that very large amounts of money were invested in all kinds of social programs in my area, Mr. Speaker, and that the population is deeply humiliated to have to accept those handouts. I say to the Department of Finance that as long as there are fiscal measures, and to the Bank of Canada that as long as there are monetary measures like those we have today, regional inequalities are going to increase in Canada. I gave statistics, Mr. Speaker, to show that the economic situation in my area has been getting worse for 15 years and the very timid efforts made for one or two years by the Department of Finance to regionalize fiscal policy are not sufficient.
Recently I asked federal and provincial civil servants in my area how many businesses have established themselves in Gaspe in the last ten years. Even though we have invested over $411 million to build roads, harbours, airports and industrial parks in that area during that period, they could not mention the name of five outside firms which had come to settle there. I would like someone to tell me why any industry would establish itself in that area, once again an area with less than 1 per cent of the total population of Canada and which is so far from the markets?
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that, all things being equal, and market pressures being what they are, no manufacturing industry will ever settle in our regions. The rationalization of the resource sectors was done at great costs. We do not think we will be able to go much further. So either we accept that our young people leave eastern Quebec at a rate of 7,000 a year, or else we innovate and do what other countries have

done, that is offer such tantalizing tax advantages that private enterprise will want to settle in those areas.
What I am suggesting is that in the budget that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) will present within two months, we try such an experiment in two or three areas which in total would represent 3 or 4 per cent of the Canadian population. I am thinking, for example, of eastern Quebec, northeast New Brunswick and maybe another region in the maritimes. Let us try this experiment. Let us drop these measures which are not only extremely costly for the government but are also a source of profound humiliation for the people. Mr. Speaker, people do not want unemployment insurance, they do not want social welfare. They want work. 1 say that in the market system we have in North America, the best one, it must be recognized that in areas far from the market, the government must introduce new policies and the tax schedule must be the same at the other end of the country as in Toronto or in Montreal. This is complete nonsense. And it is certainly not through industrial incentives which businessmen must finally pay back within three years that we are going to encourage investors to establish themselves in the maritimes or in Gaspe.
My colleague, the hon. member for Bonaventure-lles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) was telling me that the major industry now operating in New Richmond would not be there if it had not been offered considerable tax benefits at that time. It has been a decisive factor for its establishment in that area. And once again I urge the Minister of Finance to try this experience when he presents his budget next month. It would be much less costly, Mr. Speaker, than the $50 million spent each year in my constituency on unemployment insurance and social welfare. I have suggested that idea. I know that the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada are reluctant to take different financial and monetary measures, but to show you what happens when the Bank of Canada wants to ignore something and to indicate how far things have gone I would point out that the biggest and wealthiest bank in Canada, the Royal Bank of Canada, does not have even one branch in my constituency which has more than 60,000 people. How can they say that private enterprise is concerned about regional disparities when this same bank is going to open branches on every street corner in Toronto, Ottawa or Montreal, yet not a single one throughout my riding?
This demonstrates, Mr. Speaker, that it will be absolutely necessary to innovate and to reform our monetary and fiscal policies. I know that the new system will be more complicated but there is no reason why we should sink into pessimism or gloom. In the face of a difficult situation, I think that politicians should be able to react positively and the deterioration my constituency is presently going through is simply unacceptable. We have been elected on a just society platform. We promised justice at the national level to the two main ethnic groups-French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians- and justice at the economic level which will allow all Canadians to enjoy the same advantages.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have been given to understand that the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) has laid upon the table notice of the intention of the government to introduce legislation. If that is the case and if a bill is available, I wonder whether it might be available to all members of the House in order to expedite matters, and so that all members of the House know what the government's legislative intention is respecting the postal strike. We would be prepared to give unanimous consent now for the first reading of that bill, so that it could be printed and distributed immediately in order for all members of the House of Commons to be fully apprised of the government's intention.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to report to the House that this afternoon I discussed with Mr. Parrot and Mrs. Carr possible procedures which could lead to the resumption of negotiations. Mr. Parrot will have discussions with his national executive over the weekend. He has undertaken to
[Mr. De Bane.)

study these proposals. Also he has undertaken to meet with me on Monday. In light of this, I would appreciate no further action being taken until these further discussions with Mr. Parrot take place on Monday.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we all appreciate receiving the minister's statement because this is an important matter. I am sure he spoke seriously. Before he leaves, I wonder if he could tell us, whether, in the course of the discussions he has had with his colleagues, the Postmaster General and the president of CUPW, there was the assurance that postal services will be continued until Monday and while these negotiations are taking place.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the full details of the discussions which took place, but in a spirit of
Business of the House
mutual co-operation and goodwill, in order to achieve a negotiated settlement, hon. members of the House will appreciate that I cannot divulge the total conversations I have had. Indeed I have expressed the concern of members on both sides of the House regarding the fact that there has been a partial disruption of postal services, and that I was hoping these partial disruptions would cease. Obviously the union will know that the government already has served notice, if a settlement is not reached, to bring forward a piece of legislation to deal with the situation. It is my hope that this will not be necessary.
Hear, hear!
